bibliographic.title: Effective Human Oversight of AI-Based Systems: A Signal Detection Perspective on the Detection of Inaccurate and Unfair Outputs
bibliographic.authors: Markus Langer; Kevin Baum; Nadine Schlicker
bibliographic.citation_apa: Langer, M., Baum, K., & Schlicker, N. (2025). Effective human oversight of AI-based systems: A signal detection perspective on the detection of inaccurate and unfair outputs. Minds and Machines, 35(1). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11023-024-09701-0

methodology.method_family: conceptual framework applying Signal Detection Theory (SDT) to human oversight of AI-based systems
methodology.study_design: theoretical/conceptual analysis with literature-based factor synthesis; no primary empirical study reported in provided text
methodology.sector: high-risk AI decision contexts including hiring, medical decision-making, and judicial decision-making
methodology.technology_context: AI-based systems and machine learning approaches; explainable AI (XAI) referenced; no specific large language model or conversational system focus in provided text

eligibility.decision_rationale: The article directly addresses effective human oversight, error detection, fairness, risk mitigation, and high-risk regulated contexts (including EU AI Act Article 14), which align strongly with the review's governance and oversight dimensions. However, the provided text frames AI-based systems generically and does not specifically address conversational AI, chatbots, agents, RAG, or LLM-based systems; therefore it is better classified as supporting rather than central evidence for conversational LLM governance.
eligibility.manual_spotcheck_reason: Metadata year conflict (2019 vs journal 2025); confirm full-text scope for LLM/conversational specificity and whether any empirical validation is present beyond the excerpted pages.

appraisal.notes: Strong conceptual clarity and fit of SDT for explaining oversight effectiveness via sensitivity and response bias. Appraisal limited by absence of primary empirical sample or data collection in provided excerpts; authors note limited evidence interpretable from an SDT perspective on AI error detection.

cerqual.explanation: The framework is internally coherent and highly relevant to human oversight and risk reduction in regulated AI use, but confidence is moderated because the work is theoretical, cites limited SDT-applicable evidence for AI unfairness detection, and the provided text does not establish LLM- or conversation-specific applicability.

coding.theme: Conditions for effective human oversight of AI-based systems
coding.subtheme: Signal Detection Theory perspective on detecting inaccurate and unfair AI outputs

synthesis.main_claim: Reliable detection of errors—covering both inaccuracies and unfairness—is crucial for effective human oversight of AI-based systems in high-risk contexts, and Signal Detection Theory offers a useful framework for understanding what affects human sensitivity and response bias when detecting such errors.
synthesis.contribution: Extends an SDT lens to both inaccuracy and unfairness detection in AI oversight, including the need to choose a fairness standard, and synthesizes task-, system-, and person-related factors hypothesized to affect oversight effectiveness.
synthesis.limitations: Provided text indicates limited evidence that can be interpreted from an SDT perspective on detection of AI-related errors; the article is theoretical rather than empirically validating the framework, and does not address conversational or LLM-specific systems.
synthesis.use_in_review: Use as supporting theoretical evidence for governance dimensions of human oversight, error detection, fairness standards, and risk mitigation in regulated AI environments; cite cautiously for conversational LLM governance claims without additional LLM-specific mapping.
